title: C++ Essentials for DSA
relevance: Campus OAs and DSA rounds reject otherwise-correct C++ for TLE from slow I/O, silent overflow, or accidental O(n) container copies.

phases.goal: Establish the practical C++ subset that keeps DSA solutions fast, type-safe, and free of silent wrap-around.

must_hit.point: Default cin/cout sync with C stdin/stdout and cin is tied to cout, so heavy I/O can become a TLE bottleneck.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sync between C++ and C streams and/or cin flushing cout on reads as the default cost.

must_hit.point: int is 32-bit (~-2 x 10^9 to 2 x 10^9); long long is 64-bit (~-9 x 10^18 to 9 x 10^18); long long is mandatory when summing 10^5 values up to 10^9 each or multiplying two 10^9 integers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the int vs long long ranges and when long long is required for sums/products.

must_hit.point: Never pass std::vector or std::string by value unless a copy is intended; pass const& (read-only) or & (mutable) for O(1) overhead instead of O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts O(n) by-value copies with O(1) reference passing for containers.

must_hit.point: std::pair bundles two elements and std::tuple three or more; both provide lexicographical comparison, useful for sorting multidimensional data or graph edges.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names pair/tuple, how many elements each holds, and lex comparison use cases.

probes: Why can default C++ I/O alone cause TLE on large inputs, and which integer type do you reach for when products of 10^9 values appear?

hints.1: Think about what cin/cout do with C streams by default, and where 32-bit int stops being safe.
hints.2: Cover sync/tie overhead, int vs long long ranges, and when summing or multiplying forces 64-bit.
hints.3: Default sync keeps C and C++ streams aligned and cin flushes cout; int is ~±2 x 10^9 while long long is ~±9 x 10^18 and is required for 10^5 x 10^9 sums or 10^9 x 10^9 products.

phases.goal: Show how fast I/O hooks, overflow timing, buffer leftovers, and unsigned arithmetic actually behave.

must_hit.point: ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false) drops C/C++ stream sync overhead; cin.tie(nullptr) removes the automatic flush of cout before each cin read.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains both sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) and what each removes.

must_hit.point: std::endl writes a newline and forces a flush; '\n' only inserts a newline so the buffer can flush optimally.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States endl = newline + flush versus '\n' = newline only.

must_hit.point: If both operands are 32-bit ints, overflow happens before assignment to long long; cast one operand (e.g. (long long)a + b). Shifting 1 << 40 is undefined; use 1LL << 40.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers pre-assignment overflow on int+int and the 1LL << k literal fix.

must_hit.point: cin >> leaves a trailing newline; an immediate getline reads an empty string unless you consume it (e.g. cin.ignore(256, '\n')). size_t from .size() is unsigned, so size()-1 underflows when size is 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions leftover-newline + ignore/dummy getline, and size_t underflow on empty containers.

must_hit.point: double has 53 bits of precision (~15-17 decimal digits); never compare floats with ==—compare abs(a-b) against a small epsilon such as 1e-9.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives double precision bits/digits and the absolute-difference epsilon pattern.

probes: Walk through sync_with_stdio(false) plus cin.tie(nullptr), then explain why long long bad = a + b can still overflow when a and b are int.
What goes wrong if you call getline right after cin >> n, and if you write for (size_t i = 0; i < arr.size() - 1; ++i) on an empty array?

hints.1: Separate stream-speed hooks from when the overflow actually occurs in the expression.
hints.2: Explain false sync, nullptr tie, endl vs '\n', cast-before-add, leftover newline, and unsigned wrap on size()-1.
hints.3: sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) cut sync/flush cost; endl flushes every time; int+int overflows before long long store so cast one side; use 1LL << 40; ignore leftover '\n' before getline; empty size_t size()-1 wraps.

phases.goal: Judge when CP shortcuts help versus when they scramble I/O, hurt readability, or pick the wrong callable form.

must_hit.point: After sync_with_stdio(false), mixing scanf/printf with cin/cout is unsafe because the streams are no longer synchronized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns against mixing C and C++ I/O once sync is disabled.

must_hit.point: Aggressive macros (e.g. #define rep(...)) shorten code but harm readability, break scoping, and make debugging harder—use sparingly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Balances CP macro convenience against scoping/readability/debug costs.

must_hit.point: Lambdas are the usual custom comparator; functors (operator()) are still required when a type name is expected, such as the third template parameter of std::priority_queue.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts lambda instances with functor types for priority_queue.

must_hit.point: __int128 helps intermediate multiplications beyond 64-bit limits but cannot be read or printed directly via cin/cout.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States __int128 usefulness and the cin/cout limitation.

probes: When is sync_with_stdio(false) a win, and what I/O mixing rule does it impose?
When would you prefer a functor over a lambda for a custom comparator?

hints.1: Speed from desync has a compatibility cost; callables differ for types vs instances.
hints.2: Contrast desynced stream mixing, macro aggressiveness, lambda vs functor for priority_queue, and __int128 I/O limits.
hints.3: Desync speeds I/O but forbids mixing scanf/printf with cin/cout; keep macros light; use a functor type for priority_queue's compare parameter; __int128 needs manual I/O.

phases.goal: Apply the checklist patterns for input shape, safe midpoints, float printing, and recursive lambdas in real DSA code.

must_hit.point: Typical input is either read-until-EOF (while (cin >> x)) or read n then n elements into a vector.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes both EOF-stream and count-then-n reading patterns.

must_hit.point: Safe binary-search midpoint is mid = l + (r - l) / 2; (l + r) / 2 overflows when l + r > 2^31-1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the l + (r - l) / 2 form and why (l + r) / 2 fails.

must_hit.point: For floating output use cout with fixed and setprecision, or printf with a format like %.5f; stringstream is the clean way to tokenize a space-separated string or convert between ints and strings.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions iomanip fixed/setprecision or printf, plus stringstream tokenization/conversion.

must_hit.point: Recursive lambdas need an explicit signature via std::function, or a C++17 self-passing auto& trick; C++23 adds auto self.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names std::function and/or self-passing (and optionally C++23 auto self) for recursion.

probes: How do you read either EOF-terminated integers or an n-then-n-elements block, and how do you pick a midpoint in binary search without overflow?
Show a recursive DFS/fib lambda in C++17 and how you would print a double to five decimal places.

hints.1: Start from the two input shapes and the midpoint formula that avoids adding l and r.
hints.2: Cover EOF vs n-then-n, l+(r-l)/2, float formatting, stringstream tokens, and recursive-lambda typing.
hints.3: while (cin >> x) or read n then loop; mid = l + (r - l) / 2; fixed/setprecision or printf("%.5f"); stringstream for tokens; std::function or self(self, ...) for recursion.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: endl inserts a newline and forces a flush, so looping it over thousands of items can TLE; '\n' only inserts a newline and lets the buffer flush optimally.
Passing vector/string by value copies in O(n); const& gives O(1) read-only access and & gives O(1) mutable access—only pass by value when a copy is intentional.
Desyncing drastically speeds C++ streams, but then mixing scanf/printf with cin/cout scrambles I/O; alternatively scanf/printf are inherently fast and need no sync_with_stdio(false).

tradeoffs.topic: aggressive macros vs type aliases / plain code
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Short aliases like using ll = long long or all(x) are common, but aggressive #define loops break scoping, hurt readability, and complicate debugging—use sparingly.

tradeoffs.topic: lambda vs functor for custom compare
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Lambdas are the usual inline comparator; a functor type overloading operator() is required when a type name is expected, such as priority_queue's third template parameter.
Representation error makes == unreliable; compare abs(a-b) against a small epsilon (e.g. 1e-9).

gotchas.trap: Mixing scanf/printf with cin/cout after ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false).
gotchas.correction: Keep to one I/O family after disabling sync; the streams are no longer synchronized and output can scramble.

gotchas.trap: Using std::endl inside a tight output loop.
gotchas.correction: Prefer '\n'; endl flushes every iteration and can cause TLE.

gotchas.trap: Calling getline immediately after cin >> x.
gotchas.correction: cin >> leaves a trailing newline; consume it with cin.ignore(...) or a dummy getline before reading the line.

gotchas.trap: Writing long long sum = a + b when a and b are int.
gotchas.correction: Overflow occurs in the int addition before assignment; cast one operand to long long first.

gotchas.trap: Using 1 << k for a large shift such as 40.
gotchas.correction: A 32-bit literal shift is undefined behavior; write 1LL << k.

gotchas.trap: for (size_t i = 0; i < arr.size() - 1; ++i) when arr is empty.
gotchas.correction: size_t underflow turns 0-1 into a huge bound; cast to int or check empty() first.
Compare absolute difference against a small epsilon such as 1e-9.

gotchas.trap: Using (l + r) / 2 as a binary-search midpoint.
gotchas.correction: Use l + (r - l) / 2 so l + r cannot exceed 2^31-1 and overflow.
